newsitem.title: UK: Dorrell joins race to lead British Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Dorrell joins race to lead British Conservatives.

text.p: Former health secretary Stephen Dorrell on Wednesday put himself forward as a candidate for the leadership of Britain's Conservative Party, which suffered a crushing defeat in a general election last week after 18 years in power.
The struggle for the party leadership was expected to turn into a six-horse race as former Welsh secretary William Hague was scheduled to hold a news conference (0830 GMT) to declare his candidacy.
"I am standing as someone who wants to see the future rebuilt," Dorrell told the BBC.
He said he wanted "to rethink the policy position of the Conservative Party so we address the concerns of the voters directly".

So far, former finance minister Kenneth Clarke, former social security secretary Peter Lilley, former interior minister Michael Howard and arch-anti-European John Redwood have put themselves forward to succeed John Major.
Major announced he was stepping down last Friday, the morning after Tony Blair's Labour Party dealt the Conservatives their worst election defeat since 1832.

Hague, 36, has become the bookmakers' favourite since former deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine threw the race wide open by deciding he would not stand after he was admitted to hospital at the weekend due to a heart scare.
Whoever emerges as winner faces the formidable task of reuniting a Conservative Party reduced to half its size in the House of Commons by the Labour election landslide.
